meta.title: Who really said "Like two bald men fighting over a comb"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Tolstoy's coinage. He printed it in his 1874 ABC book, but the simile is an older anonymous fable — and Borges made the modern wording famous in 1983.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Like two bald men fighting over a comb'?
meta.ogDescription: Tolstoy printed the simile in his 1874 Azbuka, but he did not coin it. Quote Investigator traces the fable to Phaedrus, and the modern wording to Borges.

answer.label: Not coined by Tolstoy — an older, anonymous fable
answer.authorDates: An anonymous saying · traced by Quote Investigator to a fable recorded by Phaedrus, in French print by 1792, in Tolstoy’s Russian primer by 1874
answer.sourceLine: Tolstoy really did print the simile: it closes a short proverb-lesson on page 48 of his 1874 Azbuka (ABC Book), and from 1888 American newspapers were crediting him with it. But Quote Investigator conjectures he was sharing an existing cultural expression with anonymous provenance and did not craft the simile — a comb version was already circulating in French by 1792, and the ancestor is a fable recorded by Phaedrus. The familiar modern English wording is closest to Jorge Luis Borges’s remark on the Falklands, reported in 1983.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — Tolstoy printed it, but he did not coin it. The fable is centuries older and the origin is anonymous.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: St. Petersburg: Tip. K. Zamyslovskago, 1874 — the passage on page 48
English rendering by Quote Investigator (2019). An 1888 U.S. newspaper version reads “two bald men who fought for possession of a comb.”
Not Tolstoy’s coinage — Quote Investigator conjectures he was relaying an existing saying of anonymous provenance

source.excerpt: Two people on the street together found a book and began to argue about it. A third one asked: ‘Which of you is literate?’ They said: ‘No one; both of us are illiterate.’ Two bald men are fighting for a comb.
trail: Antiquity — a fable transmitted under the name of the Roman fabulist Phaedrus, Book 5, “The Two Bald Men”: “As on his way a Bald-pate went, / He found a comb by accident; / Another, with a head as bare, / Pursued, and hollow’d for a share.” The two men commiserate over a find neither can use — they do not fight (Perseus Digital Library ↗).

1792 — the commiseration has curdled into a brawl. In Jean-Pierre Claris de Florian’s fable Les deux Chauves, two bald men spot a glint of ivory, come to blows, and the winner loses the few grey hairs he had left — his prize is a comb (French text on Wikisource ↗). Quote Investigator documents an English translation printed in 1806 as “The Two Bald Heads.”
1874 — Tolstoy includes the simile on page 48 of Azbuka, his primer for Russian children, printed in St. Petersburg by Tip. K. Zamyslovskago (Internet Archive catalogue record ↗).

1888 onward — the Atchison Daily Champion prints the story in English and credits Tolstoy; The New York Times repeats it in 1896; H. L. Mencken files it in 1942 under “Futility” as a “RUSSIAN SAYING”; and by 1983 Jorge Luis Borges is applying it to the Falklands (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: Page 48 of Tolstoy’s Azbuka (1874), in Quote Investigator’s English rendering of the Russian. Note the shape of it: the simile is the punchline of a tiny proverb-lesson, delivered the way one delivers a saying everybody already knows — not launched as an original aphorism.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for the famous English wording: it is a proverbial simile with no identified author and no identified first work, so there is nothing to attach a copyright to. The Russian text Tolstoy printed in 1874 is long in the public domain — but the English rendering quoted above is Quote Investigator’s own 2019 translation, and belongs to its translator, not to Tolstoy.

author.name: Leo Tolstoy
author.heading: About Leo Tolstoy
author.metaLine: 1828–1910 · Russian novelist and educator — author of War and Peace and of the Azbuka primer
author.bio: Tolstoy compiled Azbuka, an ABC book for Russian children, in the same years he was writing his great novels; the Internet Archive holds a St. Petersburg printing of 1874, and page 48 carries the bald-men line as the moral of a two-sentence exchange about an illiterate pair squabbling over a book. He was working in the register of the folk proverb there, gathering sayings and riddles for children to learn from — which is precisely why Quote Investigator concludes he was relaying an expression that already existed rather than minting one. The credit stuck anyway: within fifteen years American newspapers were printing the story with Tolstoy’s name attached, and it has travelled under his name ever since.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and who has earned it
misattribution.intro: This line gets pinned on Tolstoy, on Borges, and on “an old Russian proverb” more or less interchangeably. Some of that is fair, and some of it is a translation of Tolstoy’s fame into authorship he never claimed.

items.why: He genuinely printed it — in Russian, on page 48 of the 1874 Azbuka — and American papers were crediting him with it from 1888. But Quote Investigator conjectures Tolstoy was sharing an existing cultural expression with anonymous provenance and did not craft the simile; QI’s conclusion is only that he “helped to popularize this figure of speech” (Quote Investigator ↗). Wikiquote’s Tolstoy page does not carry the line at all (Wikiquote ↗).

items.tag: He said it; he didn’t invent it
items.why: Borges applied the simile to the Falklands conflict: “The Falklands thing was a fight between two bald men over a comb.” Wikiquote sources the remark to Time, 14 February 1983 (Wikiquote ↗); Quote Investigator documents it in The Miami News of 9 February 1983. Either way the figure of speech was in English print long before he reached for it.

H. L. Mencken’s A New Dictionary of Quotations (1942) lists “Two baldhead men are fighting over a comb.” under the topic Futility, labelled simply “RUSSIAN SAYING”; James Reston used it as a Russian proverb in The New York Times in 1955 (Quote Investigator ↗). Neither treated it as anyone’s quotation.

items.scope: As a Russian invention at all
items.why: The bald men were quarrelling in French before they ever quarrelled in Russian — Florian’s Les deux Chauves has them fighting over the ivory glint that turns out to be a comb (Wikisource ↗), and the ancestor is a fable carried under Phaedrus’s name (Perseus ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s verdict: the simile evolved from the fable recorded by Phaedrus, a version about an ivory comb was circulating by 1792, Tolstoy helped popularize it in his 1874 primer, and Borges employed it by 1983 — with the original authorship staying anonymous throughout (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why the bald men changed sides
lead: Most quote sites file this under Tolstoy, and unlike the usual run of Tolstoy misattributions it is not an invention: the simile really is in his ABC book, printed for Russian children to read aloud. What is invented is the idea that it started with him.

The fable’s ancestor runs the other way round. In the version carried under Phaedrus’s name, one bald man finds a comb, a second catches up and demands a share, and the joke is that they console each other over a windfall neither can possibly use. Nobody throws a punch. Somewhere between antiquity and the eighteenth century the commiseration curdled into a brawl, and by 1792 Florian had the two of them coming to blows over a glint of ivory — the victor stripped of the last grey hairs he had, holding a comb.
context.detailsSummary: How the phrase travelled into English
detailsBody: In English the phrase travelled as a proverb rather than a quotation. Mencken filed it in 1942 under “Futility” as a Russian saying; James Reston reached for it in The New York Times in 1955 as a Russian proverb. Neither man treated it as a line with an author, which is exactly how proverbs behave.

What fixed the modern English wording was Borges. Asked about the Falklands, he produced the version people now repeat — a fight between two bald men over a comb — and the phrasing that circulates today tracks his sentence far more closely than it tracks anything in Tolstoy’s Russian. The internet has since handed Borges’s wording back to Tolstoy, which is roughly how attribution drift usually works: the more famous name absorbs the better line.
context.pull: They started out as fellow sufferers. Only later did they start fighting.
